papers.title: Sustained Activation of a Defensive Behavior-Related Circuit Elicits a distinct Homeostatic Sleep Response
papers.abstract: Animals and humans often forgo sleep in response to other physiological needs. Prolonged wakefulness leads to a compensatory homeostatic sleep response involving enhanced amounts of sleep and electroencephalographic delta (0.5-4 Hz) power, yet how the type of preceding wakefulness and brain activity affects this response is poorly understood. Here we compared the pattern of brain activity and the homeostatic sleep response following sustained wakefulness induced by either gentle handling (GH), a widely used form of sleep deprivation in rodents; or optogenetic stimulation of neurons involved in avoidance/defensive responses, basal forebrain (BF) vesicular glutamatergic transporter type 2 (vGluT2) neurons. Local infusion of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists partially attenuated the wake-inducing effect of vGluT2-stimulation, but not that of GH, suggesting mediation by other non-glutamatergic BF subtypes. These antagonists also tended to produce more NREM sleep and a shorter NREM latency in the recovery period following vGluT2-stimulation. Both manipulations increased high theta (7-9 Hz) during wakefulness, an effect partially blocked by local infusion of the glutamate antagonist cocktail. Enhanced NREM sleep time and NREM delta power in the recovery period were more pronounced following GH than following vGluT2 stimulation. Whole-brain cFos immunohistochemistry revealed stronger neuronal activity in brain regions involved in stress and avoidance/defensive behaviors with vGluT2 stimulation, compared to GH. Our results demonstrate that activation of a brain system involved in defensive behavior (BF vGluT2) elicits a distinct and diminished homeostatic sleep response compared to GH, potentially an evolutionary sleep adaptation which would maintain vigilance in the face of an ongoing threat.

papers.title: SSSI: A simulation-based framework for evaluating sigma-power fluctuation state identification pipelines in NREM sleep EEG.
papers.abstract: Sigma-band activity of the electroencephalogram during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep exhibits infraslow fluctuations. These sigma-power fluctuations (SPFs) contain recurring local waveform periods, including ascending, high, descending, and low-sigma-power portions, which can be operationally categorized as SPF states. Although some SPF states are associated with arousal-related processes and sleep fragility, how the prevalence of SPF states changes within a continuous sleep episode remains unknown. Resolving this question requires a reliable analysis pipeline, yet it has been difficult to determine which pipeline best identifies SPF states. Here, we present the Simulation of SPF and SPF-State Identification (SSSI) framework, which generates simulated SPFs with known reference SPF states and uses them to evaluate candidate SPF-state identification pipelines. With a pipeline selected through SSSI, mouse NREM and human N2 sleep showed within-episode changes in SPF-state proportions in both species, with additional age-dependent variation in humans. Pipeline evaluation further showed that the detection of these effects can depend on the pipeline. Together, these findings establish SSSI as a framework for evaluating and interpreting within-episode temporal changes in SPFs while assessing pipeline-dependent methodological bias.

papers.title: Somnus, a tunable, open-source platform for automated EEG sleep scoring in physiological and disease mouse models
papers.abstract: Many studies using mouse models of human brain disorders rely on extended recordings of brain electrical activity through electroencephalogram, or EEG. The features that researchers measure in these recordings, such as seizures and epileptiform activity, are deeply influenced by whether the animal is awake, in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, or in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Because total sleep duration varies naturally across animals, rigorous experimental comparisons require classifying the sleep state of every few seconds of a recording. Manual annotation is highly labor-intensive, often requiring hours per subject. While automated scoring tools accelerate this process, they are typically trained exclusively on healthy cohorts and frequently fail when applied to disease models that exhibit atypical or fragmented sleep architecture. Somnus is an open-source Python package designed to automate rodent sleep staging using EEG, muscle activity (EMG), and optional video-tracking data. It includes a robust base model trained on diverse recordings from six independent laboratories, enabling out-of-the-box classification across various equipment setups without requiring prior manual labeling. A central feature of Somnus is its capacity for rapid adaptation to pathological sleep structure. The software provides a graphical interface that directs researchers to the specific epochs where the base model is least certain. Users can manually correct these targeted epochs in a built-in viewer by comparing the model's classification to the raw EEG signal and video, and then use their corrections to fine-tune the model. This workflow empowers researchers to generate accurate custom scorers for complex disease models or novel treatments with just a few minutes of manual correction, bypassing the need to hand-score entire experimental cohorts or develop their own models from scratch.

papers.title: Irreversible functional network deformation induced by preprocessing scheme order in multivariate EEG recordings.
papers.abstract: The analysis of Electroencephalographic recordings is non-trivial, the order in which filtering and re-referencing are applied during multivariate signal preprocessing has a critical and underappreciated consequence for functional network estimation. Using EEG sleep recordings from healthy subjects, synthetic data from controlled numerical models (Nf-Tori and IAAFT surrogates), and surrogate-based statistical testing, we provide a quantitative comparison of two preprocessing schemes that differ solely in the order of filtering and re-referencing (filtering followed by re-referencing-FR, and re-referencing followed by filtering-RF). We show that the RF scheme induces spurious cross-correlations that increase systematically with the frequency band and are strongly modulated by the power spectral exponent β of the signal. Critically, for signals with steep power spectra (β ≥2), a regime that characterizes slow-wave sleep, epileptic post-ictal periods, anesthesia, neonatal, and patients in vegetative states, the RF scheme produces artificial correlations that are irreversible. They cannot be eliminated post-hoc even when surrogate-corrected cross-correlations (SAC-matrix) are applied. The mechanism underlying this effect is due to the high-amplitude slow-frequency components that dominate the median reference signal over extended time intervals, embedding redundant information across all channels. In contrast, the FR scheme introduces only small, systematic negative shifts in cross-correlations that are not statistically significant and can be effectively corrected using surrogate-based methods. We therefore recommend the FR scheme combined with surrogate-corrected cross-correlations for all applications involving signals with β ≥2. Although this finding is demonstrated in EEG, it applies to any multivariate recording where spatial re-referencing and band-pass filtering are applied sequentially.

papers.title: Sleep-dependent modulation of thalamic brain temperature estimates in humans
papers.abstract: Mammalian thermal physiology is geared towards dissipating heat during sleep. Brain temperature typically decreases during non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) sleep in all mammalian species measured to date, yet non-invasive confirmation in healthy humans is lacking: the only available human study used invasive recordings in epileptic patients without a wake control condition. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) enables brain temperature mapping non-invasively, using the temperature-sensitive chemical shift of water relative to N-Acetyl-Aspartate as an internal reference. First, we validated that with metabolite cycling (MC), a MRS approach that enables the simultaneous acquisition of metabolite and water information without conventional water suppression, can be used to determine estimates of brain temperature in an ex vivo sheep head. Next, we determined that by using a temporal resolution of ~4 minutes, we obtained high-quality spectra without losing excessive temporal resolution. We then re-analyzed an existing set of MRS data (acquired with the MC sequence) of the thalamus in young adults (n=9) who slept in the evening for up to 2 hours in the scanner, to assess sleep-evoked changes in estimates of brain temperature. Of the nine participants, five participants took part in the subsequent wake-only experiment, allowing to control for the potential impact of circadian time and body posture on estimates of brain temperature. Sleep-wake states were quantified with standard polysomnography, confirming that the participants managed to sleep in the scanner. On average, they spent 39.4+/-15.7 min in N2 sleep, 24.8+/-18.1 min in N3 sleep, 10.0+/-4.9 min in N1 sleep, and 37.0+/-19.6 min awake. Estimates of brain temperature were correlated across the sleep and wake-only experiment within the same participant (R^2=0.29, P<0.0001). When participants entered NREM sleep, estimates of brain temperature decreased by 0.2 degrees Celcius. Moreover, the deeper NREM sleep, the more pronounced the decrease in estimates of brain temperature (P=0.014). These data suggest that an evening nap consisting of NREM sleep decreases thalamic temperature. Considering the profound impact temperature can have on brain functioning, these brain temperature changes could be a pathway through which sleep impacts the brain.

papers.title: Hyperglycaemia reversibly disrupts circadian behaviour in mice
papers.abstract: Disrupted sleep and circadian rhythms are among the most common features of diabetes, and are known to raise the risk of developing the disease. Whether the relationship also runs the other way, with diabetes itself disrupting the clock, has remained unresolved. Using an inducible mouse model of diabetes, in which hyperglycaemia can be induced and then reversed within the same animal, we show that elevated blood glucose is a reversible cause of circadian disruption. Raising blood glucose reduced the amplitude of circadian rest-activity rhythms by 50%, in proportion to the degree of hyperglycaemia, and shortened the free-running period of the clock. Restoring normoglycaemia reversed both effects. Diabetic animals had a delayed phase of activity onset, i.e. later chronotype, and re-entrained more slowly after a simulated jet lag. However, phase shifting to nocturnal light pulses was intact, suggesting normal photic responses. Brain glucose and O-GlcNAcylation, a nutrient-sensitive protein modification, were both elevated in diabetic animals, showing that peripheral hyperglycaemia reaches the brain and alters its metabolic state, and providing a molecular readout of that exposure. Together, these findings establish that a peripheral metabolic state is a reversible determinant of circadian rest-activity behaviour, completing a bidirectional link between blood glucose and the clock and arguing that the two must be treated together rather than in isolation.

papers.title: What EEG doesn't see: a whole-brain MEG map of sleep spindles and slow oscillations
papers.abstract: Sleep spindles and slow oscillations (SOs) are hallmarks of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, linked to memory consolidation and restorative functions. They are usually detected in one or a few scalp electroencephalography (EEG) channels with parameters that vary across studies, and serve as the reference even in magnetoencephalography (MEG), fMRI and intracranial studies. We argue that these choices filter which neural activity is captured. Nineteen young adults took a daytime nap during simultaneous MEG and EEG. Using MEG source imaging across 416 cortical, subcortical and cerebellar regions, we mapped the amplitude and density of SOs (0.5-4 Hz, and 0.5-2 and 2-4 Hz separately) and of spindles (9-18 Hz, and slow, 9-12.9 Hz, and fast, 13-18 Hz, separately), and related each region's activity to a single scalp derivation (Cz-M1). Both rhythms were detected throughout the brain, including the thalamus, hippocampus, amygdala, basal ganglia and cerebellum. The balance between bands varied across regions: fast spindles predominated over slow spindles along the dorsal midline, around the central sulcus and in the thalamus, slow spindles predominated in occipital cortex and the cerebellar hemispheres, and 2-4 Hz SOs were relatively most prominent in occipital cortex. Amplitude and density formed reliable but distinct maps: regions with larger fast spindles also had more of them, whereas SOs, and slow spindles once source depth was controlled, were larger where they were less frequent. More SOs were detected in every region than at Cz-M1, whereas more fast spindles were detected at Cz-M1 than in any single region. Around the SO, slow-spindle activity had the same timing at the scalp and in the sources, but the up-state increase in fast-spindle activity seen at the scalp was absent from local sources. Slow spindles were the most strongly shared events, and sensorimotor sources the most scalp-like. Thus, a single scalp derivation offers a selective and partly composite view of sleep oscillations, with implications for interpreting their functional roles and for targeting them with closed-loop auditory stimulation

papers.title: Intersectional genetic targeting of molecularly distinct melanin-concentrating hormone neuron subpopulations reveals distinct and overlapping subcircuit architecture
papers.abstract: The lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) coordinates crucial and innate behaviors through heterogeneous yet poorly understood neuronal populations and circuits. Neurons that produce melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH; encoded by the Pmch gene) are primarily localized in the LHA and contribute to feeding, sleep-wake regulation, memory, and reward-associated behaviors. Building on foundational anatomical studies, our single-cell transcriptomic analysis of the LHA identified markers distinguishing at least two transcriptionally distinct MCH subpopulations. These subpopulations are distinguished by the selective enrichment of the Tacr3 and Cartpt transcripts, with each comprising approximately half of the total MCH population. However, these subpopulations remain poorly understood owing to limited genetic targeting tools. We hypothesized that MCH neurons operate through functionally distinct, parallel subcircuits that exhibit unique neuroanatomical projections. In this study, we leveraged Pmch and Tacr3 expression to intersectionally dissociate these neurons into Type I MCH (Pmch+/Tacr3+) and Type II MCH (Pmch+/Tacr3-) subpopulations. We first validated a Tacr3-Flpo mouse line for the genetic targeting of the Type I MCH subpopulation. We then generated an intersectional Type I MCH neuron reporter line to visualize Type I axonal projections. In parallel, we injected a dual recombinase mouse line with the intersectional genetic targeting viruses, Conditional Viral Expression by Ribozyme Guided Degradation (ConVERGD), and identified overlapping and distinct projections by Type I and Type II MCH neurons using fluorescence microscopy, super-resolution imaging, and high-spatial resolution fiber mapping. Overall, these data establish the first subpopulation-resolved anatomical framework for molecularly distinct Type I and Type II MCH subcircuits, thus establishing a foundation for future circuit-level functional studies.

papers.title: Distinct electroencephalography alpha-band rhythms map macroscale brain gradients.
papers.abstract: Brain gradients provide a low-dimensional framework for describing cortical organization, linking functional connectivity, anatomy, development, and transcriptional architecture. Whether this macroscale organization also structures fast electrophysiological dynamics remains less clear. Here we used the longstanding observation that alpha-band activity is not unitary, and that some individuals exhibit multiple alpha peaks, as an entry point for examining cortical gradients in resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). We analyzed source-reconstructed EEG from 608 adults, comprising 3,255 recordings acquired across eyes-open and eyes-closed rest before and after cognitive testing. Within individuals, parcel-wise alpha peak frequencies frequently departed from unimodality, revealing 2 separable alpha-frequency components in 38.3% of recordings. These components were not spatially arbitrary: frequency-defined clusters aligned with canonical functional networks, most prominently separating visual and somatomotor systems, although their relative frequency ordering varied across individuals. Low-dimensional analysis of cluster network composition further identified 2 principal axes: a sensory-differentiation axis contrasting visual and somatomotor contributions, and a sensorimotor-association axis resembling established functional-connectomic gradients. These findings suggest that split alpha reflects multiple sensory-anchored oscillatory modes embedded within macroscale cortical gradients, linking a classical EEG phenomenon to the brain's hierarchical architecture.

papers.title: Sleep forms flexible context representations in toddlers.
papers.abstract: Sleep consolidates episodic memory through a hippocampus-dependent process in adults. Whether and how sleep supports memory consolidation during early life, when hippocampal function is immature, remains unclear. Here, we examined effects of sleep on the consolidation of spatial context, a core component of episodic memory, in toddlers aged 2-3 years. Toddlers were familiarized with two spatial contexts, followed by a ~ 90-min nap or equivalent wake period. Afterwards, using a hide-and-seek game we tested their ability to relocate toys within these contexts. Only after post-familiarization sleep, toddlers showed significant context memory and formed stronger associations between toys and specific contexts compared to wakefulness. Contextual memory was positively correlated with spindle density and slow oscillation-spindle phase-amplitude coupling during non-rapid eye movement sleep. Here, we show that, despite hippocampal immaturity, memory effects in the sleeping toddler's brain are accompanied by thalamo-cortical oscillatory dynamics that are also implicated in adult memory consolidation.

papers.title: Protective role of high-intensity exercise and lactate against sleep deprivation-induced alterations in hippocampal gene expression and spatial learning.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation impairs cognitive function by disrupting hippocampal signaling pathways essential for memory formation. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) and lactate, a metabolic byproduct of exercise, have demonstrated potential benefits for brain plasticity, but their protective roles during sleep deprivation remain poorly understood. This study investigated the effects of six weeks of HIIT and lactate administration on memory-related gene expression and spatial learning in sleep-deprived rats. Forty-two male Wistar rats were divided into six groups: Control, Sleep Deprivation (SD), HIIT, HIIT + SD, Lactate, and Lactate + SD. After interventions, sleep deprivation was induced for 48 h. Spatial learning was assessed via the Morris Water Maze test, and hippocampal gene expression of PKA, LIMK, and cofilin was analyzed. The results showed no significant differences in spatial learning performance across groups; however, sleep deprivation caused significant downregulation of key genes involved in memory signaling. Both HIIT and lactate treatments effectively reversed these molecular impairments, notably increasing LIMK expression. These findings highlight the molecular protective effects of HIIT and lactate against sleep deprivation-induced cognitive dysfunction and suggest their potential as non-pharmacological strategies to preserve memory function under sleep loss conditions.

papers.title: Predicting ICU Seizures Using 1 hour of cEEG.
papers.abstract: Continuous electroencephalography (cEEG) is the gold standard for detecting electrographic seizures in the intensive care unit (ICU), but limited resources limit prolonged monitoring for all patients. We developed an automated, interpretable pipeline that uses a single hour of cEEG to estimate near-term seizure risk across multiple prediction windows. We retrospectively studied 50 adults who underwent ICU cEEG monitoring at a single tertiary center. From a 1-hour segment, we computed automated interictal-ictal continuum (IIC) burden probabilities for lateralized periodic discharges (LPDs), generalized periodic discharges (GPDs), and lateralized rhythmic delta activity (LRDA), along with quantitative background EEG features reflecting signal organization and hemispheric asymmetry. Segments were labeled by seizure occurrence within the subsequent 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, or 24 hours. Support vector machine (SVM) and bagged-tree classifiers were trained using clinical-only, background-only, and combined feature sets with a 70/30 patient-level train-test split and cross-validation within the training set. For the 4-hour horizon, the combined-feature SVM achieved 76% accuracy and the lowest Brier score (0.25), outperforming clinical-only (72%) and background-only (70%) models. Across horizons, SVM accuracy declined from 94% (1 hour) to 79% (24 hours) with increasing Brier scores, indicating reduced calibration at longer intervals. AUC-receiver operating characteristic increased with wider prediction windows, consistent with higher seizure prevalence at longer lead times. Integrating automated IIC probabilities with quantitative background EEG features enables moderate, interpretable near-term seizure prediction from a single hour of ICU cEEG. Initial external validation on an independent multicenter ICU cohort supports generalizability, although broader prospective and multicenter evaluation are needed before clinical deployment.

papers.title: Event-Weighted Desaturation Burden and Cardiovascular Mortality in Sleep Apnoea: Findings from a Large Community-Based Prospective Cohort.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnoea's prognostic value is limited by reliance on the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI), which fails to capture physiological heterogeneity of respiratory events. We developed a composite metric, event-weighted desaturation burden (EWDB), integrating weighted respiratory event load, regularity of consecutive inter-event intervals, and cumulative desaturation area. We evaluated its association with cardiovascular mortality and its incremental prognostic value compared with AHI and established hypoxic metrics. We analysed 4,904 adults from the Sleep Heart Health Study with baseline polysomnography and adjudicated follow-up. EWDB was derived by combining a respiratory weighted index, a distribution factor based on inter-event interval regularity, and event-linked hypoxic burden (HB). The primary outcome was cardiovascular mortality. Over a median follow-up of approximately 11 years, 341 cardiovascular deaths occurred. In fully adjusted multivariable Cox models, higher EWDB was independently associated with cardiovascular mortality. However, AHI and HB associations were attenuated and lost statistical significance after full adjustment. EWDB (per 1-SD increase) remained robustly associated with cardiovascular mortality, whereas AHI did not. Incorporating EWDB into a comprehensive clinical model provided incremental risk stratification. Similar robust associations were observed for fatal coronary heart disease and incident heart failure. EWDB was independently associated with cardiovascular mortality and provided incremental prognostic information beyond established clinical and sleep-related factors in this cohort. By integrating respiratory event intensity, cumulative burden, and inter-event interval regularity, EWDB may better characterize cardiovascular stress related to sleep-disordered breathing.

papers.title: Circadian Timekeeping in the Tropics: Rhythmic Transcriptome and Diurnal Regulatory Networks in Rubroshorea leprosula.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms allow plants to regulate internal processes to align with daily rhythms in the environment. Comparing circadian clocks across environments is essential because latitude-dependent variation in light and temperature imposes distinct selection pressures that shape the evolution and function of circadian timing systems. However, circadian clock studies have largely focused on temperate and subtropical species, leaving transcriptional circadian networks in tropical plants poorly understood. We report the comprehensive circadian transcriptome of Rubroshorea leprosula, a dominant species in tropical rainforests in Southeast Asia. One sapling was sampled every 4 hours over 48-hour period under constant darkness and used for transcriptomic analyses. Only 283 of 20 748 expressed genes (~1.3%) exhibited significant circadian oscillations, with periods strongly concentrated between 23 and 25 hours. Hierarchical clustering revealed 4 temporal clusters with alternate phases of expression and functional specialization. Comparative analysis identified clear orthologs for all major Arabidopsis circadian clock components, with conserved synteny to Parashorea chinensis, a close relative of R leprosula. Time-lagged cross-correlation network reconstruction identified a characteristic circadian topological similarity with Arabidopsis, including coupled morning and evening feedback loops and paralog expansion that maintained overall structure. Peak expression timing of these core clock genes in the tropical tree was largely consistent with that observed in Arabidopsis thaliana. In contrast, Rubroshorea orthologs showed reduced amplitudes and lower coefficients of variation under this single constant darkness, single-individual condition; because dark-induced damping is common across plants, this pattern is consistent with, but does not establish, reduced circadian robustness in R leprosula linked to tropical adaptation. This study lays the molecular foundation for circadian regulation in dipterocarps and offers a system for integrating rhythmic gene expression to ecological function and forest productivity in tropical communities.

papers.title: Circadian Rhythms in Drug Response: From Molecular Clocks to Precision Dosing.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms organize mammalian physiology across the 24-h day through molecular clocks coordinated by the central clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus and distributed to peripheral oscillators. These clocks regulate processes central to pharmacology, including drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination, and target responsiveness. Consequently, drug efficacy and toxicity can vary substantially depending on the time of administration. Despite decades of progress in pharmacogenomics and systems pharmacology, consideration of time of day remains largely absent from clinical drug development and prescription. In this review, we evaluate emerging research on circadian regulation of drug responses, considering both pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. We review chronotherapeutic strategies to treat diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, and bipolar disorder. We also discuss the use of wearable technologies to enable time-resolved drug evaluation. Finally, we discuss the challenges to clinical translation and the integration of circadian timing into precision medicine and optimized dosing strategies.

papers.title: Time-of-Day Variation in Knee Extensor Strength and Fatigue Is Associated With Circadian Phenotype in Healthy Young Adults.
papers.abstract: Time-of-day variation in neuromuscular performance is well established, but the contribution of circadian phenotype remains unclear. This study examined whether maximal knee-extensor strength and fatigue resistance differ between morning and evening and whether chronotype and actigraphy-derived sleep-timing are associated with diurnal performance variation. Forty-four healthy young adults (21 males, 23 females) completed a randomised-crossover protocol consisting of neuromuscular testing in the morning (0700-0900) and evening (1700-1900). Participants completed 7 days of actigraphy monitoring and the Composite Morningness Questionnaire to characterise behavioural circadian phenotype. Sleep timing was assessed using habitual sleep midpoint (between sleep-onset and wake-time), with night-to-night variability in sleep midpoint used as an index of sleep-timing variability. Maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) torque, fatigue index, contractions completed, and time-to-exhaustion were assessed during each trial. Baseline MVIC torque was greater in the evening compared with the morning (2.96 ± 0.80 vs 2.85 ± 0.77 N m kg⁻1; P < .0001), with post-fatigue torque also remaining higher in the evening (2.00 ± 0.60 vs 1.84 ± 0.54 N m kg⁻1; P < .0001). Participants demonstrated a lower fatigue-index (32.57 ± 6.99 vs 35.58 ± 6.26%; P < .0001), completed more contractions (37.95 ± 8.29 vs 35.09 ± 7.58; P < .0001), and exhibited longer time-to-exhaustion (6.36 ± 1.51 vs 5.85 ± 1.26 minutes; P < .0001) during evening testing. Chronotype was strongly associated with the PM-AM difference in MVIC torque (r = -.684, P < .0001), explaining 47% of the variance in diurnal performance responses. Neither habitual sleep midpoint (r = -.029, P = .848) nor night-to-night variability in sleep midpoint (r = -.055, P = .721) was associated with performance differences. No significant sex-related differences were observed. Maximal knee extensor strength and fatigue resistance were enhanced during evening compared with morning testing. The magnitude of this response was strongly associated with behavioural circadian phenotype, but not actigraphy-derived sleep-timing. Findings suggest that chronotype influences time-of-day differences in neuromuscular performance and should be considered when evaluating exercise performance.

papers.title: Effects of General Anaesthesia on the Sleep Structure of Patients With Prolonged Disorders of Consciousness.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common in patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness (pDoC) and are closely correlated with clinical outcomes. With an increasing number of pDoC patients undergoing surgery under general anaesthesia (GA), this study characterized sleep patterns in pDoC patients and evaluated the effects of GA on consciousness and nocturnal sleep. We prospectively enrolled 30 pDoC patients (14 in vegetative state [VS] and 16 in minimally conscious state [MCS]) undergoing spinal cord stimulation and 12 healthy controls. Among pDoC patients, 19 (10 VS, 9 MCS) with complete pre- and postoperative PSG data were analysed for GA effects. Controls underwent one overnight polysomnography (PSG); pDoC patients underwent pre- and postoperative PSG. Consciousness was assessed with Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R) before and after surgery. Compared with controls, pDoC patients presented significantly impaired sleep structure, including reduced total sleep time (TST), decreased NREM Stage 2 sleep, diminished slow-wave sleep (SWS), reduced rapid eye movement (REM) sleep duration and percentage relative to TST (all p < 0.05). No significant short-term changes in CRS-R scores were observed following GA. Although GA significantly prolonged TST (p = 0.039), with numerical increases in absolute NREM and SWS durations, no statistically significant changes were observed in sleep stage percentages relative to TST (all p > 0.05). Subgroup analysis showed no significant within-group changes in sleep stage percentages in either the VS or MCS group. These findings suggest that GA increases TST without statistically significant changes in sleep structure in pDoC patients.

papers.title: An Explainable Self-Supervised Temporal Transformer for Participant-Level Classification of Depressive Symptoms From Resting-State EEG.
papers.abstract: Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive modality for investigating depressive symptoms; however, conventional deep-learning methods often require large labeled datasets and provide limited interpretability. We developed an Explainable Self-Supervised Temporal Transformer Network for participant-level classification of BDI-defined elevated depressive symptoms from resting-state EEG. The framework employed masked temporal modeling for self-supervised pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning. Model performance was evaluated using repeated nested participant-wise cross-validation and compared with conventional machine-learning and deep-learning baselines. Explainability was investigated through transformer attention maps and SHAP-based channel attribution. The proposed model achieved a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.73-0.90), a precision-recall AUC of 0.69, balanced accuracy of 0.75, sensitivity of 0.72, and specificity of 0.78. The positive predictive value was 0.57, indicating a substantial false-positive burden in the evaluated cohort. The proposed model showed the highest point-estimate ROC-AUC among the evaluated baselines, with a 0.07 improvement over EEGNet; however, the overlapping uncertainty intervals and the small elevated-symptom cohort warrant cautious interpretation of comparative superiority. Performance decreased from an ROC-AUC of 0.82 in Run 1 to 0.78 in Run 2 and to 0.72-0.73 under cross-condition transfer, supporting interpretation of these analyses as internal reproducibility and condition-shift assessments rather than independent external validation. Removing self-supervised pretraining reduced the ROC-AUC to 0.74. Explainability analyses identified distributed temporally relevant intervals and frontal-midline to centro-parietal channel contributions, with attribution interpreted as model-relevance evidence rather than causal biomarker evidence. Overall, the findings provide preliminary internal evidence that self-supervised temporal representation learning can support participant-level classification of BDI-defined elevated depressive symptoms from resting-state EEG under the evaluated experimental conditions. The findings do not establish clinical diagnostic validity, screening readiness, or independent external generalizability.

papers.title: Effects of morning versus evening high-intensity exercise on electroencephalographic and autonomic responses in middle-aged women.
papers.abstract: The time of day at which exercise is performed influences physiological responses and performance, and thus its health benefits. This study investigated whether electroencephalographic (EEG) and autonomic nervous system responses to morning versus evening exercise differed in middle-aged women. Thirty women aged 50-60 years were randomly assigned to a morning or evening exercise group. Participants were asked to sleep for seven to eight hours before testing. The morning group exercised at 6:00 am and the evening group at 6:00 pm. EEG-derived indices included the theta-to-beta ratio (TBR) and spectral edge frequency at 90% (SEF-90). Photoplethysmography-derived autonomic indices comprised the HRV index and HRV-derived sympathetic-related and parasympathetic-related indices, measured at rest before and immediately after exercise. Data were analyzed using a two-way mixed-design analysis of variance. For significant interactions, simple effects and change-score analyses were performed. TBR and SEF-90 showed significant group × time interactions, with greater changes from pre- to post-exercise in the morning group. TBR increased and SEF-90 decreased following exercise in both groups, with greater changes in the morning group. The HRV index showed only a significant main effect of time. However, HRV-derived sympathetic-related and parasympathetic-related indices demonstrated significant group × time interactions, with greater autonomic responses in the morning group, as measured by change scores. EEG- and HRV-derived neurophysiological response patterns to high-intensity exercise may vary with exercise timing. Morning high-intensity exercise may elicit greater neurophysiological responses than evening exercise, highlighting the importance of exercise timing in training strategies and recovery.

papers.title: Impact of environmental enrichment and allostatic load induced by repeated mixing on the transcriptome of three porcine brain tissues.
papers.abstract: Environmental enrichment and mixing represent two management procedures in pig production with opposing effects: while environmental enrichment can promote welfare by reducing stress, repeated mixing often induces stress and can negatively impact welfare. Despite their importance in pig husbandry, how these opposing management procedures affect brain function at the molecular level remains poorly understood. This study investigated how environmental enrichment and allostatic load induced by repeated mixing influence gene expression patterns across three porcine brain regions: hypothalamus, prefrontal cortex, and hippocampus. Using RNA sequencing, we analyzed brain tissues from 48 gilts subjected to a 2 × 2 factorial design comparing enrichment conditions (enriched vs. barren) and allostatic load (repeated vs. minimal mixing). While environmental enrichment showed minimal impact on gene expression, allostatic load resulted in 38 differentially expressed genes in the hippocampus, primarily involved in hormone regulation, protein transport, and neuronal activity. Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) identified modules moderately correlated with experimental conditions: six modules in hippocampus associated with allostatic load, and four modules in hypothalamus associated with enrichment. Functional annotation revealed that these modules were primarily enriched in biological processes related to synaptic signaling, neuron development, and metabolic activity. Hub genes from these modules were identified, and turned out not to overlap with differentially expressed genes. Our findings suggest that based on this experimental design, the hippocampus may be particularly responsive to stress-induced transcriptomic changes, while the molecular effects of the environmental enrichment appear more subtle. Overall, this study reveals limited but region-specific transcriptional responses to allostatic load in the porcine brain.

papers.title: Vascular brain injury modifies the relationship between sleep duration, cognition, and white matter hyperintensity burden in the Alzheimer's disease continuum.
papers.abstract: Self-reported sleep duration is associated with dementia-risk and vascular brain injury markers, including white matter hyperintensities (WMHs), yet how additional cerebrovascular pathology alters these relationships remains unclear. In a deeply phenotyped cohort (735) including healthy and Alzheimer's disease (AD) continuum individuals (subjective and mild cognitive impairment [MCI], dementia [AD], MCI and AD with high vascular burden [+V]), sleep was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Individuals were classified as WMH-only or WMH+ (WMHs with microbleeds, infarcts, or cerebral amyloid angiopathy). Linear models tested interactions between sleep duration, WMH+ status, and diagnostic group on WMH burden and cognition. In MCI+V and AD, WMH+ significantly amplified the association between shorter sleep and greater WMH burden. In AD, longer sleep related to better cognition in WMH+ but worse cognition in WMH-only (exploratory). Additional vascular brain injury modifies how sleep relates to WMH burden and cognition across the AD continuum, highlighting the importance of moving beyond WMHs alone.

papers.title: The link between inflammation and autonomic dysfunction in alpha-synucleinopathies - narrative review.
papers.abstract: Alpha-synucleinopathies are a group of disorders characterized by the accumulation of the pathological form of alpha-synuclein. This group comprises Parkinson's disease, Parkinson's disease dementia, multiple system atrophy, dementia with Lewy bodies, pure autonomic failure, and idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder. Despite sharing a similar molecular basis, these disorders differ in their clinical presentation. Characteristic manifestations include signs of autonomic failure such as orthostatic hypotension, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, constipation, gastroparesis, urinary incontinence, and erectile dysfunction, among others. These symptoms significantly impair patients' daily functioning and are also negative prognostic factors. Currently, research is investigating the link between inflammation and dysautonomic symptoms. Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, and IFN-α, have been found to accompany these symptoms. Notably, in other diseases characterized by chronic inflammation, autonomic dysfunction is also common. In two human studies of dysautonomic symptoms in other conditions, intravenous immunoglobulin therapy was shown to improve these symptoms. Animal studies have shown that other immunomodulatory agents reduce symptom severity. Modulation of inflammation, dietary modification, the use of probiotics and prebiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation are potential therapeutic approaches for these diseases. These approaches offer hope for improving the quality of life of patients with alpha-synucleinopathies. Further research in this area is needed.

papers.title: Cardiac fibrosis and heart failure: Metabolic stress, circadian dysregulation, and extracellular matrix remodeling.
papers.abstract: Diabetes is a major risk factor for heart failure and drives a distinct cardiomyopathic phenotype characterized by oxidative stress, metabolic inflexibility, mitochondrial dysfunction, and progressive myocardial remodeling. Central to this process is cardiac fibrosis, marked by excessive extracellular matrix deposition, increased myocardial stiffness, and impaired mechanotransduction. Emerging evidence identifies circadian rhythm disruption as an under recognized modifier of diabetic cardiac fibrosis. The circadian clock regulates daily oscillations in myocardial metabolism, redox balance, inflammatory signaling, and extracellular matrix turnover, thereby maintaining cardiac homeostasis. However, modern urbanization has introduced chronic exposure to artificial light at night, particularly blue light from digital devices, which suppresses melatonin and desynchronizes central and peripheral clocks. In diabetes, loss of circadian regulation amplifies TGF-β signaling, Rho-A/ROCK-mediated mechanotransduction, oxidative stress, and myofibroblast transformation. Understanding how circadian misalignment accelerates profibrotic remodeling may reveal novel chronotherapeutic strategies to reduce cardiac fibrosis and heart failure risk.

papers.title: Migration Characteristics and Mechanism of Active Components From Jieyu Anshen Granule in Different Insomnia Mouse Models.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a highly prevalent disorder with substantial health and socioeconomic impacts, for which traditional Chinese medicine is an important treatment option. Jieyu Anshen Granule (JYAS-G) shows excellent clinical efficacy in insomnia treatment, but its active components, in vivo migration characteristics and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Two mouse insomnia models induced by p-chlorophenylalanine (PCPA, chemical method) and sleep deprivation machine (SDM, physical method) were established respectively, and mice were administered with low and high doses of JYAS-G, with open field test used to evaluate the pharmacodynamic effects. UHPLC-Q-Orbitrap-MS combined with GNPS was applied to systematically identify the in vitro components of JYAS-G and its migration profiles in mouse plasma, liver, heart, prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and hypothalamus. The SDM model induced insomnia with manic-like behaviors, which were significantly ameliorated by JYAS-G, whereas the PCPA model produced no significant insomnia-like phenotypes under the current conditions. In total, 89 in vitro components and 43 blood-absorbed components of JYAS-G were identified, showing marked tissue-specific distribution. Network pharmacology and molecular docking identified core components, including furanogermenone and curcumenol, predicted to exert anti-insomnia effects by targeting ADORA2A, GABRB3, and SLC6A4 and regulating the neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction pathway. This study characterizes the in vivo migration characteristics of JYAS-G and provides insights into its multi-target anti-insomnia mechanism, while comparing the modeling differences between two common insomnia animal models. These findings provide scientific evidence for the rational clinical application and further development of JYAS-G.

papers.title: Ligustilide enhances TNTs-mediated mitochondrial transfer to accelerate the reactivation of TECs in sleep deprivation induced postpartum mouse.
papers.abstract: Angelica sinensis (Oliv.) Diels (Danggui) has been widely used by puerperae in China for postpartum recovery for more than a thousand years. Its key active ingredient, ligustilide (LIG), has been documented to exert thymus-repairing effects; however, its role and underlying mechanisms in postpartum thymic regeneration impairment remain unclear. During the puerperium, the acutely atrophied maternal thymus gradually returns to its non-pregnant state. However, frequent sleep deprivation (SD) resulting from neonatal breastfeeding often slows down the thymus recovery process. This study investigated the efficacy and underlying mechanism of LIG, an active ingredient of A. sinensis, against SD-induced thymic regeneration disorder (SDTRD) in postpartum mice. Postpartum SD was induced by automated disturbance; a progesterone-estrogen withdrawal (PE) model followed by a 7-day high-dose steroid treatment. LIG (1 mg/kg) was administered during regeneration. Thymic architecture (H&E), thymic epithelial cells (TEC) localization (immunofluorescence), and thymocyte subsets (flow cytometry) were quantified. Spleen sjTREC, thymic cytokines, and transcripts for mitochondrial biogenesis/function were measured by qPCR. TEM assessed mitochondrial ultrastructure. Dual-color mitochondrial tracing combined with a thymocyte-iTECs co-culture system and a bone-marrow-cell thymic homing assay mapped intercellular mitochondrial transfer. Tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) were disrupted with cytochalasin D; Rho-GTPase activation (including Cdc42) was evaluated. Postpartum mice with SD showed damaged mitochondrial ultrastructure and reduced mitochondrial biogenesis in TECs, leading to TECs dysfunction and interruption of postpartum thymic regeneration. LIG significantly restored the abnormal spatial localization of TECs, improved the reticular framework of cortical TECs (cTECs), promoted thymocyte development, and increased output of CD4+ T-cells. Mechanistically, LIG may facilitate the formation of F-actin-dependent TNTs between thymocytes and TECs, mediating mitochondrial transfer from thymocytes to dysfunctional TECs. This process may rely on Rho GTPase signaling pathways (Cdc42 activation) to regulate F-actin polymerization. LIG may promote F-actin-dependent TNTs-mediated mitochondrial transfer from thymocytes to TECs, thereby reactivating TECs, restoring the thymic microenvironment, rescuing thymocyte development and export, and ultimately ameliorating SD-induced postpartum thymic regeneration. These findings provide new experimental evidence for the development of LIG as a preventive and therapeutic intervention for defective postpartum thymic repair.

papers.title: Cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation in pediatric epileptic syndromes: mechanisms, limitations, and future research horizons.
papers.abstract: Drug-resistant epilepsy affects approximately 20 to 30% of children with epilepsy, with particularly devastating outcomes in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs). Cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation (c-tDCS) has emerged as a promising noninvasive neuromodulation approach warranting systematic evaluation. Recent meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials demonstrate significant reductions in seizure frequency following c-tDCS compared with sham stimulation, corresponding to roughly 3 to 4 fewer seizures per month or a proportional reduction of about 45% at 4 weeks. Evidence supports efficacy in focal epilepsies and selected syndromes, including Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and early-onset epileptic encephalopathies. Standard protocols employ 1 to 2 mA cathodal stimulation for 20 minutes over 5 to 10 consecutive sessions. High-definition tDCS configurations allow more focal current delivery. However, significant inter-individual variability exists, and the relationship between interictal epileptiform discharge suppression and clinical seizure outcomes remains inconsistent. Computational modeling demonstrates substantially higher cortical electric field strengths in children than in adults at equivalent current intensities, raising important dosing considerations. Safety data from over 600 pediatric sessions indicate favorable tolerability with no serious adverse events, although seizure exacerbation has been reported in a minority of participants in open-label studies. Cathodal tDCS represents a safe, tolerable, and potentially effective adjunct to unchanged antiseizure medication regimens in children with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and should presently be regarded as investigational. Selection criteria, optimal stimulation parameters, and syndrome-specific protocols require further refinement. Particular caution is warranted with transcranial alternating current stimulation in generalized epilepsies. Research priorities include closed-loop electroencephalography (EEG)-triggered stimulation systems, biomarker- driven patient selection, age-appropriate dosimetry informed by computational modeling, and adequately powered trials in specific DEE populations including West syndrome, Dravet syndrome, and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation during sleep.

papers.title: Real-time wearable detection of respiratory infections in pediatric transplant households
papers.abstract: Consumer-grade wearables can continuously and longitudinally measure health signals such as heart rate (HR), activity, and sleep. While changes in these signals have been implicated in the early detection of infection (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2) and real-time alerting systems have been developed, evidence from prospective deployment in pediatric transplant households remains limited. Here, we study the application of a resting heart rate (RHR)-based real-time alerting algorithm to detect respiratory virus infection in a cohort of solid organ transplant recipients and their household members (n=146) in a Phase IV clinical trial (NCT06161454). Reliable and efficient alerting for infection events may be particularly relevant for this population, enabling isolation, clinical management, and/or treatment. Of 31 antigen-test outcomes, nearly all (29/31, 93.5%) correspond to either influenza, COVID, or other patient-reported symptoms. We describe RHR, HR, activity, and sleep/circadian rhythm features around clinical alarm events, identifying candidate features for further investigation and algorithm improvement.

papers.title: Attenuated attention engagement and sensorimotor resonance to social events in first-episode adolescent depression: Evidence from EEG oscillations.
papers.abstract: Depressive symptoms may disrupt social brain development during adolescence, resulting in adverse long-term quality of life. Yet, little is known regarding the cognitive and neural changes during the processing of social interactions in adolescents with first-episode depression, particularly from an allocentric perspective. We used electroencephalography (EEG) to assess two neural indicators during the observation of others' interactions, including sensorimotor mu suppression and occipital alpha-band activity, in 22 adolescents with first-episode major depressive disorder (MDD) and 23 healthy counterparts. Participants observed animated motions wherein actions were directed toward animate (human-like) or inanimate (rock) targets, comprising social (giving) and kinematically matched control events (disposing, taking and acquiring). Healthy controls (HCs) exhibited stronger central-parietal mu suppression in the lower sub-band during observation of socially interactive giving events than disposing events. In contrast, adolescents with MDD manifested no corresponding difference in mu suppression. Additionally, depressive adolescents demonstrated significantly higher occipital alpha power when viewing social (patient) than non-social (rock) targets, and this alpha power was significantly higher than that observed in HCs. Exploratory correlation analyses revealed that attenuated sensorimotor resonance of social interactions was significantly associated with increased severity of depressive symptoms in the MDD group. Adolescents with first-episode depression showed difficulties in efficiently encoding social information and implicitly extracting the social-relational meaning of observed social interactions. These findings critically extend current understanding of neurocognitive mechanisms underlying social cognitive alterations in this population, and provide potential avenues for early screening and targeted interventions of social functioning impairment in adolescence.

papers.title: The Association of Window Ventilation Frequency with Depressive Symptoms Among Older Chinese People: Perceived Sleep Duration and Psychological Resilience.
papers.abstract: Little is known about the potential mechanism of window ventilation behavior on depressive symptoms in older people. Associations between window ventilation frequency and depressive symptoms were investigated with modified Poisson regression using the 2018 data of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS), with 11,374 Chinese adults aged 65 years and over. Serial mediation models were applied to investigate if self-reported total sleep duration and psychological resilience mediated the association between window ventilation frequency and depressive symptoms. Window ventilation frequency was negatively associated with depressive symptoms. The mitigating effect of high window ventilation frequency on depressive symptoms had the highest efficacy in spring and the lowest in winter. Window ventilation frequency also had a significant link with depressive symptoms through three significant mediating pathways: the mediating role of self-reported total sleep duration, the mediating role of psychological resilience, and the mediating role of self-reported total sleep duration and psychological resilience, separately. Findings of this study highlighted the mechanism that connects window ventilation behavior to depressive symptoms in older adults.

papers.title: [Tiaoshen acupuncture for shift work circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder: a randomized controlled trial].
papers.abstract: To observe the clinical efficacy of Tiaoshen (regulating the mind) acupuncture for shift work circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (SWD). A total of 84 patients with shift work circadian rhythm SWD were randomly divided into a Tiaoshen acupuncture group (42 cases, 1 case dropped out) and a non-meridian non-acupoint group (42 cases, 2 cases dropped out). Both groups received sleep health education as basic treatment. The Tiaoshen acupuncture group was treated with Tiaoshen acupuncture, Baihui (GV20), bilateral Fengchi (GB20), Touwei (ST8), Shenmen (HT7), Zusanli (ST36), as well as auricular points Shenmen (TF4), Xin (CO15) were selected. The non-meridian non-acupoint group received shallow needling at non-meridian non-acupoint points, as well as non-related auricular points. Both groups were treated 3 times per week for 4 weeks. Before treatment, after treatment, and after 3 months of treatment completion, the morningness-eveningness questionnaire (MEQ), Pittsburgh sleep quality index (PSQI), self-rating anxiety scale (SAS), and self-rating depression scale (SDS) were used to assess the sleep and emotional status in the two groups. Compared before treatment, the MEQ scores were increased after treatment and after 3 months of treatment completion in the two groups (P<0.001, P<0.01); the scores of PSQI, SAS and SDS were decreased after treatment and after 3 months of treatment completion in the Tiaoshen acupuncture group (P<0.001), and the scores of SAS and SDS were decreased after treatment in the non-meridian non-acupoint group (P<0.01). After treatment and after 3 months of treatment completion, the MEQ scores in the Tiaoshen acupuncture group were higher than those in the non-meridian non-acupoint group (P<0.001), and the PSQI scores in the Tiaoshen acupuncture group were lower than those in the non-meridian non-acupoint group (P<0.001); after treatment, the SAS and SDS scores in the Tiaoshen acupuncture group were lower than those in the non-meridian non-acupoint group (P<0.05, P<0.01). Tiaoshen acupuncture can effectively improve the sleep-wake rhythm and sleep quality of patients with shift work circadian rhythm SWD, alleviate the accompanying anxiety and depression.

papers.title: Shift work and hormonal-circadian disruption raise urinary incontinence: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Pelvic floor dysfunction (PFD) is a multifactorial condition that affects a large proportion of women, compromising urogenital support and producing symptoms such as urinary incontinence (UI). The structural and functional integrity of the pelvic floor depends on coordinated interactions among muscular, hormonal, and neuroendocrine systems. Evidence indicates that circadian misalignment, particularly in women exposed to night-shift work, sleep deprivation, and endocrine disruption, can influence pelvic floor physiology through melatonin suppression, cortisol dysregulation, and inflammatory activation. This review intends to synthesize current evidence on the links between circadian rhythm disruption, hormonal imbalance, and PFD, with specific emphasis on occupational shift work as a model of chronic chronobiological stress, highlighting their integrated pathophysiological mechanisms and preventive approaches. We conducted a narrative literature review using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science covering the period from January 2020 to October 2025. Studies investigating the relationship between circadian regulation, hormonal modulation, and pelvic floor function were included. Particular attention was given to research addressing melatonin and cortisol pathways, estrogen modulation, and occupational factors such as night-shift work, sleep deprivation, and physical overload. Eligible study designs included randomized controlled trials, observational studies (cross-sectional and cohort studies), translational and experimental research, and high-quality mechanistic reviews, defined by methodological rigor, comprehensive literature synthesis, and critical appraisal of evidence. Circadian rhythm disruption-characterized by decreased melatonin secretion, altered cortisol levels, and increased oxidative stress-has been associated with inflammation, impaired muscle contractility, and delayed pelvic floor tissue repair. Beyond anatomical alterations, UI is increasingly recognized as a neuroimmunoendocrine disorder in which hormonal dysregulation contributes to tissue instability and loss of urethral support. Women exposed to night-shift work, sleep deprivation, or occupational overload show higher rates of involuntary urine loss, partly mediated by endocrine desynchronization and maladaptive voiding behaviors during chronically misaligned biological rhythms. Preventive measures include supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy, optimization of sleep hygiene, correction of work schedules, and local estrogen therapy when indicated. Chronobiological and immunomodulatory interventions have recently emerged as promising adjunctive strategies. Management of UI should move beyond a purely mechanical perspective toward an integrated model encompassing hormonal, metabolic, and behavioral modulation. Understanding the interactions among circadian rhythms, endocrine control, and pelvic tissue physiology may open innovative avenues for prevention and treatment, promoting precision-based, holistic care in women's health.

papers.title: AcNR1F orchestrates epidermal remodeling to enable host adaptation in Angiostrongylus cantonensis.
papers.abstract: Nuclear receptor NR1F regulates circadian rhythms in mammals, metamorphosis in insects, and molting in free-living Caenorhabditis elegans; however, its role in parasitic nematode development remains elusive. Angiostrongylus cantonensis, a zoonotic pathogen that causes eosinophilic meningitis in humans, exhibits distinct host adaptation, with mice and most mammals serving as non-permissive hosts and rats as the permissive host. We combined multi-omic analyses, lentivirus-mediated RNAi, LC-MS/MS, and dual-luciferase assays to elucidate AcNR1F functions in development and host adaptation. Acnr1f was expressed in the intestine, uterus, and seminal vesicle by in situ hybridization. Acnr1f showed high expression in L5 larvae and adults but low expression in L1-L4 larvae. Acnr1f expression was significantly higher in worms derived from rats than from mice; approximately 25% of co-expressed genes (918) were identified as potential downstream targets that may be integrated to regulate parasitic adaptation. RNAi reduced Acnr1f transcripts by 38.11% in female adults, resulting in significantly decreased recovery of L4 and L5 larvae and adults, a 64% reduction in egg production, and abnormal eggs with low hatching rate. Histological and ultrastructural analyses revealed thinned cuticle, reduced collagen fibers, and disrupted epidermal integrity. Transcriptomic analysis showed that differentially expressed genes were enriched in structural constituent of cuticle, metalloendopeptidase activity, extracellular matrix structural constituent. Dual-luciferase assays showed that the down-regulated collagen genes col-12 and col-144 were direct AcNR1F targets (>300-fold and >40-fold induction, respectively). Differential levels of cholesterol, corticosterone, and 7α,25-dihydroxycholesterol between worms from rats and mice were identified as AcNR1F ligands by LC-MS/MS and ligand-binding assays. Thus, AcNR1F is a ligand-activated nuclear receptor that directly regulates target genes to influence development and reproduction of A. cantonensis. The distinct availability of host-derived ligands and differential AcNR1F expressive level between worms from rodents highlights this receptor as a critical molecular switch for parasitic adaptation, providing mechanistic insights into host-pathogen interactions.

papers.title: Sustained Seizure Freedom After Stereo-Electroencephalography Without Definitive Intervention: Evidence for Network Modulation by Invasive EEG.
papers.abstract: Stereo-electroencephalography (sEEG) is a diagnostic technique used to localize seizure-onset networks in drug-resistant epilepsy, typically guiding resection, ablation, or neuromodulation. Sustained seizure freedom after diagnostic implantation alone is rarely described. We describe two patients who achieved long-term remission after sEEG monitoring without definitive surgical intervention. A 39-year-old man with posttraumatic right hemispheric epilepsy underwent implantation of 11 depth electrodes, during which no habitual seizures were captured despite medication withdrawal and provocation. After electrode explantation, he discontinued all antiseizure medications and has remained seizure-free for 71 months. A 63-year-old woman with left temporal epilepsy underwent implantation of 12 depth electrodes; monitoring again failed to capture habitual seizures, although abundant mesial temporal interictal discharges were recorded. After explantation, which was complicated by a small tract hemorrhage, she has remained seizure-free for 20 months on stable cenobamate therapy. These cases add to a limited body of evidence suggesting that sEEG implantation may induce microlesional or network-modulatory effects capable of interrupting seizure propagation, analogous to remission reported after intracranial electrode placement in prior series. Recognition of this phenomenon is clinically important. When no habitual seizures are recorded and early postoperative improvement is observed, a period of extended follow-up may be warranted before pursuing resection, ablation, or neuromodulation. Further study is needed to define predictors of remission, clarify underlying mechanisms, and guide patient counseling regarding this uncommon but meaningful effect of invasive EEG.

papers.title: From localized to long-range: functional connectivity alterations in mild to moderate chronic low back pain patients.
papers.abstract: Mild pain can influence brain function, yet its central neurobiological mechanisms in chronic low back pain (CLBP) remain insufficiently defined. This study aimed to quantitatively evaluate localized and long-range functional connectivity (FC) alterations in patients with mild to moderate CLBP using static/dynamic regional homogeneity (sReHo/dReHo) and seed-based FC, and to assess their statistical relationships with clinical pain and psychological metrics. A total of 55 mild to moderate CLBP patients and 39 healthy controls (HCs) underwent 3.0 T resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) and clinical assessments, including Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Short-Form of the McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ), Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). sReHo and dReHo (sliding window =50 TRs, step size =5 TRs) maps were computed to identify abnormal localized brain regions. Brain regions showing significant group differences were selected as seeds (6-mm spherical regions of interest, ROIs) for whole-brain FC analysis. Statistical comparisons were corrected using Gaussian random field (GRF) theory (voxel-level P<0.005, cluster-level P<0.05). Partial correlation analyses were used to control for age, sex, education, and head motion (Bonferroni-corrected threshold P<0.007). Compared with HCs, patients exhibited significantly reduced sReHo in the third cerebellar vermis (peak t=-4.253, GRF P<0.05), alongside reduced dReHo in the right parahippocampal gyrus (t=-4.796, GRF P<0.05) and left inferior temporal gyrus (t=-3.935, GRF P<0.05). Seed-based FC analysis revealed decreased connectivity between the third cerebellar vermis and right hippocampus (t=-4.678, GRF P<0.05), and increased connectivity between the left inferior temporal gyrus and left pallidus (t=4.441, GRF P<0.05). Patients showed significantly higher SAS anxiety scores (25.15±5.01 vs. 23.08±2.18, P=0.008). Correlation analyses demonstrated that sReHo in the third cerebellar vermis was negatively correlated with SAS scores (r=-0.384, P=0.005), whereas FC between the left inferior temporal gyrus and left pallidus was positively correlated with SF-MPQ sensory (r=0.381, P=0.006), affective (r=0.386, P=0.005), and total scores (r=0.445, P=0.001). Patients with mild to moderate CLBP exhibit distinct localized and long-range FC alterations within cerebello-hippocampal and cortico-basal ganglia pathways. These neurofunctional changes may contribute to the integration of subjective pain dimensions and comorbid anxiety. Combining static/dynamic ReHo with seed-based FC provides complementary neurobiological insight into how low-intensity chronic pain may affect the central nervous system and highlights the importance of early clinical recognition.

papers.title: An Exploratory Retrospective Comparison of Crisugabalin and Pregabalin Among 12-Week Treatment Completers With Postherpetic Neuralgia.
papers.abstract: Pregabalin (PGB) is commonly used for postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), but its clinical effectiveness may be limited by insufficient pain relief or adverse events (AEs). Crisugabalin (CGB) is a novel α2δ-1 ligand that has demonstrated efficacy in randomized placebo-controlled trials. However, comparative real-world evidence for CGB and PGB remains limited. This single-center retrospective cohort study included patients with PHN who completed at least 12 weeks of CGB or PGB monotherapy between January and June 2025. In October 2025, a single structured telephone interview was conducted to retrospectively assess patients' recalled status at treatment initiation (T0) and at Weeks 1, 4, and 12. Outcomes included the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and the physical and mental component summary scores of the 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36). Linear mixed effects models (LMMs) were designated as the primary analyses and adjusted for age, sex, pain location, pre-enrollment pain duration, hypertension, and diabetes. Repeated measures analysis of variance and the LMM analysis based on inverse probability weighting of propensity scores were performed as sensitivity analysis. Safety outcomes were descriptively assessed among treatment completers. A total of 113 patients were included, including 56 in the CGB group and 57 in the PGB group. In the adjusted LMMs, significant treatment-by-time interactions were observed for NRS scores (p < 0.001), PSQI scores (p < 0.001), and SF-36 mental component summary scores (p = 0.003), the extent to which these three scores of the CGB group improved over time may be higher than that of the PGB group. The treatment-by-time interactions were not statistically significant for SF-36 physical component summary scores (p = 0.377). Sensitivity analyses using repeated measures analysis of variance produced concordant findings for NRS, PSQI, and SF-36 mental component scores but not for SF-36 physical component scores. At least one AE was reported by 11 of 56 patients in the CGB group and 18 of 57 patients in the PGB group, but there was no overall significant difference in AEs (p = 0.196). Among patients who completed 12 weeks of treatment, the CGB group was associated with statistical differences to some extent in NRS, PSQI, and SF-36 mental component scores than PGB group, and these degree of improvement over time may be more pronounced. Due to the substantial bias in retrospective studies and the relatively small sample size, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory, merely have reference value, and require more confirmation in prospective controlled studies in the future.

papers.title: The Neural Symphony in the Periodontium: Health, Inflammation, and Regeneration.
papers.abstract: Periodontal nerves, comprising sensory, sympathetic, and parasympathetic fibers, are essential components of the periodontium. Beyond their classic sensory and proprioceptive functions, these neural networks actively modulate periodontal immune responses, bone remodeling, and tissue regeneration. They orchestrate tissue homeostasis by releasing specific neuropeptides, neurotransmitters, and neurotrophic factors. The progression of periodontitis is intimately linked to neural dysregulation, where proinflammatory mediators (e.g., excessive substance P and sympathetic catecholamines) overpower protective signals (e.g., calcitonin gene-related peptide and parasympathetic acetylcholine). Conversely, successful periodontal regeneration requires the restoration of this neural equilibrium. Nerve terminals rapidly sprout into osteogenic zones during early repair. Subsequently, their spatiotemporally patterned signaling suppresses osteoclastogenesis and promotes the osteogenic differentiation of stem cells. Crucially, these local neural networks function as a bidirectional conduit linking the periodontium to the central nervous system: systemic stressors (eg, sleep deprivation and chronic stress) can compromise ganglionic autophagy or trigeminal function to exacerbate periodontal bone loss, while periodontal pathogens can reciprocally exploit these pathways to induce central neuroinflammation. Recognizing this interconnected oral-neural-brain axis not only explains why certain periodontitis-susceptible patients remain refractory to conventional therapies but also highlights the broader impact of periodontal inflammation on neurodegenerative risk. Furthermore, nerve-targeted strategies, including neurotrophin-functionalized biomaterials, local neuropeptide delivery, and bioelectric neuromodulation, offer promising approaches to resolving refractory inflammation, restoring periodontal integrity, and concurrently mitigating the risk of associated central neuroinflammation. In this review, we comprehensively characterize the spatiotemporal plasticity of periodontal nerves under physiological and pathological conditions. We dissect the molecular mechanisms linking neural signaling to periodontal immunity and repair, and highlight how integrating neurobiology into periodontology could advance the development of next-generation regenerative medicine.

papers.title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Multiple Sclerosis: A Topical Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: The glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (RAs) are a relatively new class of drugs that were initially approved by the US Food and Drug Administration to improve glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and, subsequently, weight reduction in patients with obesity. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is commonly associated with comorbidities for which GLP-1RAs are indicated. An increasing prevalence of comorbid chronic diseases has increased the number of people living with MS (pwMS) who are prescribed a GLP-1RA, for indications of obesity, diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea, metabolic-associated steatohepatitis, and/or chronic kidney disease. This review addresses the following key considerations: (1) the use of GLP-1RAs for weight loss in pwMS and obesity, including considerations related to drug tolerability and safety; (2) the efficacy of the GLP-1RAs for their approved non-MS indications in pwMS; and (3) the potentially pleiotropic effects of the GLP-1RAs on the MS disease course beyond their approved indications.

papers.title: Acute Onset Orolingual Choreoathetosis and Auditory Hallucinations in a Healthy Young Adult Following High Melatonin Dose.
papers.abstract: Melatonin is considered a safe OTC sleep aid with rarely reported adverse effects despite limited data. We present a case of acute orolingual choreoathetosis and auditory hallucinations following 132 mg ingestion of melatonin in an otherwise healthy, 22-year-old active-duty male in IBOLC training. The patient developed abrupt, predominantly orolingual choreoathetosis and mild auditory hallucinations, 1 hour after waking. Three days earlier, he began taking 24 mg of melatonin nightly for insomnia and ingested 132 mg the night before presentation. He denied alcohol, illicit drug, or other medication use. On ED arrival, he was hemodynamically stable with continuous orolingual choreoathetosis. Initial labs demonstrated mild acute kidney injury and transaminitis. Head CT was unremarkable. MRI head showed a nonspecific left frontal white matter hyperintensity. Lumbar puncture revealed normal protein and WBC, negative culture, and negative oligoclonal bands, though CSF processing difficulties prevented autoimmune panel completion. Neurologic symptoms resolved by the next morning without recurrence, and a subsequent EEG was unremarkable. This case documents a temporal association between high-dose melatonin exposure and acute neurologic symptoms but does not establish melatonin as the cause. The clinical presentation also occurred in the setting of substantial confounders, including sleep deprivation and heat exposure. This observation supports further investigation of uncommon neurologic presentations occurring after high-dose melatonin intake.

papers.title: Virtual reality as a metacognitive training tool for lucid dreaming.
papers.abstract: Lucid dreaming (LD) involves awareness of being in a dream during REM sleep and depends on the reactivation of metacognitive and reality-monitoring processes. This study tested whether a virtual reality (VR) intervention designed to rehearse lucid-dream-relevant metacognitive routines increases LD rates beyond baseline training, and whether generic VR exposure produces similar effects. Thirty-eight participants with low previous LD experience completed a 5-week program of daily dream diaries and reality checks, assigned to: VR-experimental (n = 13), standard training plus eight LucidDreamingVR sessions preceded by brief open monitoring (OM) meditation; VR-control (n = 12), standard training plus eight LD-unrelated VR sessions; or Control (n = 13), standard training only. Dreams were classified as ordinary, semi-lucid, or lucid; semi-lucid and lucid dreams were treated as lucid-like. VR-experimental participants reported the highest number of lucid like dreams (26), followed by Control (11) and VR-control (4). A Poisson model with total recalled dreams as offset showed that lucid-like dream rates were significantly higher in VR-experimental than in VR-control, RR = 8.60, 95% CI [3.00, 24.64], p_Holm <0.001, and Control, RR = 4.00, 95% CI [1.97, 8.09], p_Holm <0.001. Responder rates showed a convergent pattern, with at least one lucid-like dream reported by 84.6% of VR-experimental participants, 61.5% of Control participants, and 33.3% of VR-control participants, showing that VR exposure alone was insufficient. Dream-oriented VR training preceded by OM meditation may facilitate LD by scaffolding metacognitive monitoring from wakefulness to REM sleep.

papers.title: Predictors of Activity and Concentration Interference in Adults with Migraine: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
papers.abstract: Objective: To identify demographic and daily cognitive, affective, and contextual predictors of headache-related interference with activity and concentration in a smartphone-based migraine cohort, using statistical models appropriate to the ordinal structure of patient-reported interference. Background: Migraine burden extends beyond headache to encompass cognitive and affective disturbance, yet most disability instruments summarize functioning retrospectively and cannot capture day-to-day variability in interference. Ecological momentary assessment addresses this limitation, yet few studies have examined cognitive and affective correlates of interference independent of pain intensity or have modeled interference using methods that respect its ordinal, non-equal-interval structure. Methods: From May 2025 to April 2026, adult participants were enrolled in this prospective, decentralized observational study via specialty clinics and social media campaigns. Eligibility required fulfilling ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria for migraine using a validated electronic survey and experiencing between 3 and 20 monthly headache days. Enrolled individuals recorded daily smartphone diary entries and performed three brief cognitive tests over a 30-day monitoring period. Daily interference with activities and concentration were captured on 5-point ordinal scales and analyzed via cumulative link mixed-effects models incorporating participant-specific random intercepts. Predictor selection across nested specifications relied on likelihood ratio testing and Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) metrics, prioritizing the more parsimonious model when goodness-of-fit was comparable. Results: The analytic sample comprised 1,267 headache-day observations from 143 participants. In the final models, brain fog (OR = 2.49 for activity, 3.19 for concentration), forgetfulness (OR = 1.48, 1.65), and mood disturbance (OR = 1.19, 1.31) were each independently associated with both outcomes (all p < 0.01), while age, sex, and employment status showed no significant association with either. Sleep quality (OR = 0.86) and anticipated next-day enjoyment (OR = 0.81) provided additional explanatory value for activity interference (p < 0.05) but not for concentration interference, for which the three-predictor model of brain fog, forgetfulness, and mood alone was retained as the most parsimonious final model. Conclusions: Cognitive and affective symptoms, rather than demographic or socioeconomic characteristics, are the primary correlates of headache-related functional interference in this cohort. Activity and concentration interference are explained by partially distinct sets of daily influences, supporting the clinical value of assessing cognitive and affective symptoms alongside conventional pain-focused evaluation.
